← Glucose HUD case study

ENGINEERING NOTE · DATA FRESHNESS

A prediction is only as good as its last reading.

Glucose HUD warns about a low before it happens by projecting the last 20 minutes forward. Getting the maths right was the easy part. The harder part was deciding when not to show a warning.

System
CGM → relay → phone → G2
Horizon
30 minutes ahead
Validation
28 automated tests

01 · THE PROBLEM

By the time you look, the reading is already old.

A glucose sensor doesn’t stream. Dexcom and Nightscout give a reading every few minutes, and LibreLinkUp’s history only has a point every 15 minutes. So when you glance at the glasses, the newest number might be from a few minutes ago.

The obvious approach is to project the trend forward from the time of that reading. But then, if the last reading is four minutes old, the warning is four minutes late. And if the sensor stops sending for a while, the old trend keeps predicting from data that no longer says anything about the person.

02 · THE FIX

Project from now, and only from fresh data.

The rate comes from a least-squares line through the last 20 minutes of readings. When there are only two sparse points, as with LibreLinkUp, it falls back to the change per 5 minutes. Anything slower than 0.5 mg/dL a minute counts as steady, so it doesn’t warn.

The projection starts from the current time, not the reading time. It only warns if the line crosses your low or high threshold within 30 minutes; past that, a straight line is mostly noise. It also says nothing when the newest reading is 15 minutes old or more, or when you’re already low, because the status line already shows that.

const cur = currentReading(pts)
if (!cur || isStale(cur.at, now)) return null
let rate = slopePerMin(pts, 20)
if (rate == null && cur.deltaMgdl != null) rate = cur.deltaMgdl / 5
if (rate == null || Math.abs(rate) < 0.5) return null
// Project from "now", not from the reading time.
const elapsed = (now - cur.at) / 60_000
const projected = cur.mgdl + rate * elapsed

03 · HOW I TESTED IT

Testing when it warns, and when it doesn’t

The prediction code is plain functions with no screen or network involved, so the tests feed in made-up readings and check the exact number of minutes.

  • Falling 2 mg/dL a minute from 110 shows “LOW in ~20 min”.
  • The same readings with the newest one 4 minutes old show 16 minutes instead.
  • Rising readings warn about a high instead.
  • No warning when the numbers are steady, the low is far away, the data is stale, or you’re already low.
  • Two LibreLinkUp points 15 minutes apart still give a warning, at about 23 minutes.
  • In demo mode, the falling person triggers a predicted low and the steady one doesn’t.

04 · WHAT IT DOESN’T COVER

It’s something to glance at, not an alarm.

Even Hub has no background or push API, so nothing can warn you while the plugin is closed. A straight line also can’t know about a meal or a correction dose, which is why it only looks 30 minutes ahead. The app says clearly that it isn’t a medical device: check your meter or CGM app before making treatment decisions.

The same rule applies to any pipeline that makes a call from recent data. Check how old the data is before you use it, and show nothing rather than a confident answer built on stale numbers.
